A.explanation: Diffraction is spreading through a gap or around an obstacle and occurs for both transverse waves and longitudinal waves such as sound.

B.explanation: Polarisation restricts oscillations to one plane perpendicular to travel, which is only possible if oscillations are transverse to the direction of travel.

C.explanation: Reflection at a boundary obeys the law of reflection for both transverse waves and longitudinal waves such as sound.

D.explanation: A stationary wave forms by superposition of two progressive waves and can be formed from longitudinal waves as in a sound tube as well as transverse waves on a string.

hints: Notice the word cannot, so test each of diffracted, polarised, reflected and stationary against the definition of a longitudinal wave.
Recall that in a longitudinal wave the oscillations are parallel to energy travel, while in a transverse wave they are perpendicular to energy travel.
Recall what polarisation does to the plane of oscillation and ask why that process needs a choice of perpendicular directions.
walkthrough: Identify the test: a longitudinal wave has particle or field oscillations parallel to the direction of wave travel, while a transverse wave has oscillations perpendicular to travel.
State the rule for polarisation: polarisation selects or restricts the transverse oscillations to a single plane, so it requires oscillations with more than one possible perpendicular direction.
Apply this to a longitudinal wave: its oscillations are along the single line of travel, so there is no perpendicular plane to restrict and it cannot be polarised.
Check the other processes: diffraction, reflection and formation of a stationary wave by superposition do not require transverse oscillations and occur for sound, which is longitudinal.
Therefore only a polarised wave must be transverse and cannot be longitudinal. This is option B
